patterns.name: 1D State DP
patterns.explanation: Define `dp[i]` = answer for the prefix ending at i (or for some 1-dimensional sub-problem indexed by i). Transition computes `dp[i]` from `dp[i-1]`, `dp[i-2]`, etc. Often optimizable to O(1) space with rolling variables.
patterns.when_to_use: Climbing Stairs, House Robber, Maximum Subarray (DP form of Kadane), Minimum Cost Climbing Stairs, Decode Ways, Word Break, Longest Increasing Subsequence (O(N²) DP form).
patterns.intuition: When the optimal answer at index i depends only on a small number of earlier indices, scan forward and accumulate. The state must capture *everything* a future transition could need.
common_pitfalls: Insufficient state — `dp[i]` doesn't carry enough info for the transition
Off-by-one between 'index i' and 'first i elements'
Initializing dp[0] / dp[1] incorrectly
Forgetting that 'maximum subarray' can be negative if all elements are negative

patterns.name: 2D Grid DP
patterns.explanation: DP on an R × C grid where `dp[r][c]` depends on neighbors (typically up and left). Common transitions: sum of paths, minimum/maximum path, count of unique paths, Cherry Pickup (bidirectional).
patterns.when_to_use: Unique Paths (I, II, III), Minimum Path Sum, Triangle, Cherry Pickup, Dungeon Game, Maximum Square. Whenever the problem is on a grid and the answer at (r, c) depends on a few neighbors.
patterns.intuition: Each cell is a subproblem; the grid order ensures dependencies are computed first. Often you can collapse to a single row when only the previous row is needed.
common_pitfalls: Iterating in the wrong order so dependencies aren't yet computed
Initializing the boundary row/column incorrectly
Using O(R·C) space when O(C) suffices
Confusing 'count paths' (additive) with 'min path' (min)

patterns.name: 0/1 Knapsack
patterns.explanation: Each item can be taken at most once. `dp[i][w]` = best value using first i items with total weight ≤ w. Transition: take or skip. Optimizable to 1D by iterating weights *backward*.
patterns.when_to_use: Partition Equal Subset Sum, Target Sum, Last Stone Weight II, Ones and Zeroes, Profitable Schemes. Recognizable when each item has 'choose / don't choose' and a capacity constraint.
patterns.intuition: Backwards iteration on the 1D form prevents re-using the same item by accident. Forward iteration would let item i contribute to multiple positions in one sweep — that's unbounded knapsack.
common_pitfalls: Forward iteration on 1D when 0/1 was required → effectively unbounded knapsack
Using boolean DP when integer counts are needed
Forgetting the empty-knapsack base case
Capacity dimension too large for memory (use offset / sum-difference reformulation)

patterns.name: Unbounded Knapsack & Coin Change
patterns.explanation: Each item can be taken any number of times. 1D DP, iterate weights *forward* so each item contributes to higher capacities multiple times in one sweep.
patterns.when_to_use: Coin Change (min coins, count ways), Combination Sum IV, Perfect Squares, Word Break (DP form), Integer Break.
patterns.intuition: Items are reusable, so when computing `dp[w]`, building from `dp[w − item]` (already updated this round) is correct.
common_pitfalls: Confusing 'count ways' (combinations vs. permutations) — outer loop order matters
Backwards iteration when forward was needed (becomes 0/1)
Initializing 'min coins' to 0 instead of +∞
Returning -1 vs. throwing for 'impossible' cases

patterns.name: LIS & LCS
patterns.explanation: Longest Increasing Subsequence: O(N²) DP, or O(N log N) with patience-sort + binary search. Longest Common Subsequence: 2D DP `dp[i][j]` = LCS of prefixes.
patterns.when_to_use: LIS, Russian Doll Envelopes, Number of LIS, Longest Common Subsequence, Edit Distance, Distinct Subsequences, Shortest Common Supersequence.
patterns.intuition: LIS-O(NlogN) maintains 'patience piles' — the i-th pile's top is the smallest tail of an LIS of length i+1. Binary search for placement gives O(log N) per element.
common_pitfalls: Using O(N²) when N = 10^5 (TLE)
Confusing 'subsequence' with 'substring'
Patience sort: confusing the pile tops with an actual LIS (it isn't — it just gives the length)
Off-by-one in the 2D LCS DP base row/column
patterns.complexity_signature: LIS: O(N log N). LCS: O(N · M).

patterns.name: Edit Distance & String Alignment
patterns.explanation: Levenshtein distance: insertions, deletions, substitutions. `dp[i][j]` = edit distance between prefixes. Generalizes to weighted operations and alignment scoring.
patterns.when_to_use: Edit Distance, One Edit Distance, Delete Operation for Two Strings, Minimum ASCII Delete Sum, Wildcard Matching, Regular Expression Matching.
patterns.intuition: Three operations correspond to three predecessors in the DP table. Match: take diagonal directly; mismatch: take min(diagonal, up, left) + 1.
common_pitfalls: Allowing simultaneous insert+delete that double-counts
Wildcard `*` matching — careful about empty matches and greedy expansion
Forgetting to initialize the first row/column with the trivial costs
Mishandling case sensitivity
patterns.complexity_signature: O(N · M) time, O(min(N, M)) space

patterns.name: Interval & Partition DP
patterns.explanation: DP on intervals `[i, j]` where the transition picks a split point `k` inside the interval. `dp[i][j] = best over k of f(dp[i][k], dp[k+1][j])`. Classic O(N³) shape.
patterns.when_to_use: Burst Balloons, Matrix Chain Multiplication, Minimum Cost to Cut a Stick, Stone Game II / III / VII, Strange Printer, Palindrome Partitioning II.
patterns.intuition: When solutions are built by combining results of two adjacent sub-intervals, iterate by increasing interval length so smaller subproblems are solved first.
common_pitfalls: Iterating by `i, j` without ordering by length → using uncomputed states
Burst Balloons: thinking forward (which to burst first) instead of backward (which to burst LAST)
Confusing partition DP with prefix DP
O(N³) is fast for N ≤ 500; for larger N, look for Knuth optimization

patterns.name: Bitmask DP & Tree DP
patterns.explanation: Bitmask DP: state = subset of N items (N ≤ 20). Tree DP: state = subtree, transitions combine children. Both extend the basic DP framework to non-linear structures.
patterns.when_to_use: Bitmask: TSP (Held-Karp), Smallest Sufficient Team, Partition to K Equal Sum Subsets, Maximum Compatibility Score Sum. Tree: House Robber III, Diameter, Binary Tree Cameras, Counting Subtrees.
patterns.intuition: Bitmask DP enumerates subsets explicitly (only feasible for N ≤ 20). Tree DP computes per-subtree answers postorder; each node combines children's answers based on whether the node itself is 'taken' or 'free'.
common_pitfalls: Bitmask state too large (2^N · N = 2^25 already 33M — borderline)
Tree DP returning a single number when the parent needs two (e.g., 'with/without current')
Iterating bitmasks in the wrong order so transitions use uncomputed states
Trying tree DP on graphs with cycles
